newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma seeks new premier, faster reforms.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma seeks new premier, faster reforms.

text.p: Ukraine's President Leonid Kuchma was in the unsettling position of seeking a sixth prime minister in as many years of independence on Thursday, although he said after the last one resigned that faster reforms were on the way.

In the short term, it seemed Kuchma's acceptance of Pavlo Lazarenko's resignation on Wednesday could please Western investors, who had accused Lazarenko of doing too little to speed up privatisation and stop constant demands for bribes.

"Kuchma said a new phase in the activity of government had begun and that reforms would now be carried out more actively," his spokesman said on Wednesday. "Government itself should be restructured," he was quoted as saying.
Pavlo Lazarenko's descent from power surprised few, though its timing, as Ukraine fought to pass a budget, shocked some.
His links with the energy sector and accusations -- which he denies -- that he raked in millions of dollars from Ukraine's biggest gas trader were used as ammunition by his critics.
That and his failure to speed up reforms, especially privatisation, were often mentioned in private to Kuchma by Western officials irritated at the slow pace of reforms.

Analysts say Western officials and business people and Ukrainian reformers had been demanding his head for months. They pointed to Kuchma's apparent reluctance to sack Lazarenko outright as a sign he feared his political and financial clout.

Some analysts believe that Lazerenko's admission to hospital on June 19 -- for reasons that are still unclear -- was negotiated with Kuchma as a way for him to leave the premiership without losing face. Both men are from the Dnipropetrovsk industrial region, home to many Ukrainian political heavyweights.
"This was the most acceptable compromise, where they both pretend to believe he's sick. Kuchma thought Lazarenko was too powerful to take on head-on," one analyst said.

Some aides said Lazarenko was fine, one said he was suffering from "exhaustion" and the chief doctor at the hospital where he has been a patient since June 19 said he was suffering from a severe and dangerous form of varicose veins.
Few believe Lazarenko has left Ukraine's political stage forever, and he is seen as a potential candidate for presidential elections scheduled for October 1998.

It was unclear if his departure would influence the International Monetary Fund, which is discussing fading prospects for a quick delivery of a three-year $2.5-$3 billion loan needed to continue reforms launched by Kuchma in 1994.
The Fund said after parliament took almost six months to pass the budget that it might issue an interim stand-by loan as about 10 conditions of a wish list of 41 are still to be met.
Reformist, centrist and nationalist deputies in parliament on Wednesday were clearly relishing prospects of a change to a prime minister with smaller political ambitions.
In the meantime, Lazarenko's deputy Vasyl Durdynets is acting prime minister and Kuchma has decreed the cabinet should keep working. He has 60 days to appoint a replacement.
Kuchma met parliamentary leaders on Wednesday to discuss a replacement. That would need approval from 226 deputies in the 450-seat chamber which is due to close in mid-July to September.
No clear favourite had emerged late on Wednesday from a long list of possibles which included Ivan Plyushch, a former parliamentary speaker with a reputation for sharp wit.
